issue.title: codex-imagegen: add a CLIProxyAPI backend for image generation
issue.body:
## Request

Add a CLIProxyAPI execution branch to `skills/creative/codex-imagegen`. A user whose Codex session routes through CLIProxyAPI should be able to generate assets with the proxy's Images API when the native `image_gen` tool is unavailable.

Treat this as an execution backend alongside the existing Codex-native path. Preserve the flat, layered, and spritesheet modes and their artifact contracts.

## Current behavior

`SKILL.md` requires a Codex CLI with an authenticated ChatGPT session and tells the agent to stop when that prerequisite is absent. `reference/api-key-path.md` points to the external Codex system skill's script and describes `OPENAI_API_KEY` as a prerequisite.

In the tested T3 setup, the Codex shadow home uses API-key authentication for CLIProxyAPI. `features.image_generation = true` is set, but Codex filters out the native image tool because of its provider/authentication gate. CLIProxyAPI can still fulfill image requests directly.

## Verified experiment

Tested on 2026-09-05 with T3 Code 0.0.38, Codex CLI 0.153.4, and CLIProxyAPI 7.2.148:

- `GET /v1/models` advertised `gpt-image-2` and `gpt-image-1.5`.
- The existing bundled system imagegen CLI successfully called `http://127.0.0.1:8317/v1/images/generations` with `gpt-image-2`.
- The SDK used `OPENAI_BASE_URL` for the gateway URL and `OPENAI_API_KEY` for the existing gateway key. No separate OpenAI Platform key was needed.
- The gateway key was read from the configured Codex shadow home's `auth.json` and passed in the subprocess environment. No credentials were printed or committed.
- A prompt for a blue ceramic robot holding an orange flower produced a visually correct PNG in 25.3 seconds.
- Requested `1024x1024`, quality `low`; received **1122x1402**, 1,824,369 bytes. Quality metadata was not captured.

This proves one successful generation. It does not prove editing, native T3 tool restoration, or reliable size/quality control.

## Implementation requirements

- Add explicit backend selection and document when to choose CLIProxyAPI. Keep the existing native route available.
- Accept a configurable gateway URL and credential source. Reuse an existing configured proxy key without requiring a paid OpenAI Platform key. Do not hard-code this machine's paths.
- Keep gateway authentication distinct from upstream ChatGPT OAuth. Never overwrite Codex login state or change T3/proxy settings as part of generation.
- Call the proxy's Images API directly for generation and decode its returned image into the existing artifact pipeline. Avoid the native-tool transcript extraction path for this backend.
- Default to `gpt-image-2`; do not silently change models or providers on failure.
- Preserve immutable version families, sequential batches, partial layered-run evidence, chroma-key processing, and spritesheet validation. Propagate backend selection through layered requests and spritesheet generation.
- Verify actual image dimensions after decoding. Report mismatches; define any resizing/cropping policy explicitly rather than claiming the backend honored the requested size.
- Return clear failures for an unavailable gateway, invalid credentials, unsupported model, upstream timeout, or missing/malformed image data. Avoid unbounded retries or silent provider fallback.
- Update `SKILL.md` and `reference/api-key-path.md` to distinguish a gateway key from an OpenAI Platform key. Remove claims that this route is deterministic about size or that subscription-backed generation is inherently free.
- Ship the implementation and dependencies from this repo. If reusing the system imagegen CLI, follow the repo's vendoring and credit rules rather than depending on an evolving external installation path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A configured CLIProxyAPI backend generates and saves a real image while the Codex native image tool is unavailable.
- [ ] Generation works with the existing gateway key and without a direct OpenAI Platform key.
- [ ] Flat, layered, batch, and spritesheet-generation entry points retain their artifact and versioning contracts.
- [ ] Tests cover backend selection, request/auth construction, response decoding, dimension mismatch reporting, and actionable error handling without exposing secrets.
- [ ] A live smoke test records the requested model/dimensions, actual image dimensions, artifact path, and visual inspection result.
- [ ] The native route remains usable, and no login or provider configuration is mutated.

## Research

- [CLIProxyAPI #4194: Image generation unavailable in Codex Desktop with gpt-5.6-sol](https://github.com/router-for-me/CLIProxyAPI/issues/4194). A near-identical missing-tool report was resolved with local ChatGPT login and separate proxy bearer configuration.
- [CLIProxyAPI #4273: Valid image results remain in generating state](https://github.com/router-for-me/CLIProxyAPI/issues/4273). Discussion distinguishes local tool exposure from server-side injection; a collaborator recommends OAuth login mode.
- [Codex #24465: Allow custom providers to opt into image generation](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24465). Open request documenting the client-side API-key authentication gate.
- [Codex #36832: App exposes image_gen while CLI filters it out](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/36832). Open report of the same custom-provider symptom across Codex surfaces.
- [Codex #28723: Image generation ignores size and quality](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/28723). Open report consistent with the observed dimension mismatch.
- [CLIProxyAPI #4309: gpt-image-2 generation fails around 120 seconds](https://github.com/router-for-me/CLIProxyAPI/issues/4309). Maintainer attributes EOF failures to upstream timeouts and declines automatic retries because they can duplicate generation work. Not encountered in this smoke test.
- [Codex 0.153.4 image-tool gate](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.153.4/codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs#L699).
- [CLIProxyAPI Codex configuration guide](https://help.router-for.me/agent-client/codex). OAuth mode may restore the native tool while retaining proxy routing. That alternative was researched but not tested; it is outside this API-branch ticket.

issue.title: Simplify the development skill family, refresh staffing, and add CLIProxyAPI images
issue.body:
The software development family now follows one ticket through groom, shape, build, merge, and retro. Groom reads all open issues, preserves native dependencies during consolidation, and routes clear work directly to ready. Milestones group testing batches; approved spec splits define integration branches. Shaping and builds use secondary worktrees, recover pushed branches, and preserve ownership and checkpoints across machines.

Build owners implement and fix inline, obtain independent code review and risk-appropriate verification, publish inspected evidence outside Git, and open ordinary PRs for human selection. Reports identify the tested integration tree. Merge checks current approval and shaping holds, honors configured branch protection and checks merge freshness without requiring protection, and preserves active or unique work during cleanup. Retro saves a pending batch of local session versions and presents project issue drafts for user selection.

Instructions remove redundant negations, routine command recipes, duplicate policy, and arbitrary diagnosis and diagram rules. Label setup uses a compact table. The worktree helper skill and Relay are retired. Standalone worktree guards, prelaunch reservations, bounded review, isolated headless browser verification, and human approval boundaries remain. Staffing assigns Astra to planning and execution, Fable 5.1 to taste and frontend design, and Terra to bounded collection and capture.

Fixes #208: the bundled image adapter selects configured CLIProxyAPI, then native Codex, then direct OpenAI API with an available Platform key and explicit authorization. Native results must belong to the launched session; generation and sprite extraction use the same chroma key. Artifact publication rejects occupied or symbolic targets. T3 retains worker identity through ambiguous responses or credential-cleanup failures, and auth/naming waits are bounded.

The visual family guide, manual review order, and adversarial report describe the final contracts and remaining eval plan. The mobile Markdown reader exposes all 385 package files across the unchanged 36-skill install set and preserves internal links. The original reviewer reports remain as historical evidence.

Validation:

- 72 offline helper tests pass: 6 artifact-branch, 32 dispatch/naming, and 34 image-backend tests. New failure regressions were demonstrated red before their fixes.
- Sprite acceptance covers 14 criteria plus bounds sanity; the versioning dry run passes.
- Three fresh independent reviews closed additional authority, symbolic-ref, response-decoding, and embedded-motion findings. A headless browser check confirms two motion figures operate independently with one shared controller.
- Metadata and dependencies pass for all 46 authored skills; the 36-skill install closure and runtime package boundaries pass. Formatting and diff checks pass.
- Mobile/desktop report checks pass; all 385 reader sources load and 2,034 local links and anchors resolve. Earlier live CLIProxyAPI smoke returned an inspected image and correctly reported its dimension mismatch.

Behavior will be assessed through actual work in integrations-v2 after installation and reconciliation, as selected by the user. Synthetic agent fixtures are retired as a rollout gate. Live native-format compatibility, T3 failure recovery, repository merge behavior, and Linux browser isolation remain capability-specific observations to establish where used.

`backlog build` drains the initial frontier: ready-for-agent tickets with no open blockers, admitted under global ownership and capacity rules. A selected approved spec or milestone advances through successive waves, preserving branch targets and human merge selection. Worker deadlines bound waits; queue and tracker checkpoints support resume. Review-ready PRs remain distinct from confirmed delivery completion.

performed_via_github_app.name: Socket Security
performed_via_github_app.description:
### Socket protects your app from malicious dependencies lurking in your open source supply chain.

Open source code makes up 90% of most codebases. It is critical to manage it effectively to reduce your security risk.

## Detect and block open source supply chain attacks

Security teams depend on Socket to prevent malicious open source dependencies from infiltrating their apps.

Socket dramatically improves your open source security posture by _detecting and blocking the attacks you don't expect_ – malware, install scripts, hidden code, typo-squatting, and more – which aren't caught by traditional vulnerability scanners.

- **Block malware** – Block emerging malware threats

- **Block typo-squatting** – Block malicious packages that differ in name by only a few characters, and recommend the correct package

- **Detect hidden code** – Detect obfuscated, minified, or hidden code

- **Detect privileged API usage** – Report when a dependency update introduces new risky API usage – filesystem, network, child_process, eval()

- **Detect suspicious updates** – Sudden inclusion of privileged APIs in patch or minor releases

Socket currently [supports 80+ detections](https://socket.dev/alerts) in 5 categories: supply chain risk, quality, maintenance, known vulnerabilities, and license problems.

## Take charge of your dependency health

Socket improves security outcomes and reduces work for security teams by **surfacing actionable security information directly inline in GitHub** so developers are empowered to make better decisions.

- **Five minute deployment** – The easiest security product you'll ever deploy in your organization. Just install a GitHub app and you're done.

- **Provide security feedback directly on PRs** – Empower developers to solve security issues before they're deployed into production.

- **Automated security** – Spend security team resources auditing the highest-impact dependencies, instead of all or nothing.

## Socket detects what vulnerability scanners can’t

It's no longer sufficient to scan for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and stop there. And yet, that's what the leading "supply chain security" products do, leaving you vulnerable.

It can take weeks or months for a CVE to be discovered, reported, and detected by tools. But in today's culture of fast development, a malicious dependency can be updated, merged, and running in production in days or even sometimes hours.

Defenders need a new approach to address emerging threats from malicious dependencies:

- **Maintainer intentionally added malware** – Rogue maintainer sabotaged his own open source package with 100M downloads/month, affecting companies such as Amazon AWS

- **Package hijacked and poisoned w/ cryptominers and password-stealing malware** – Deliberate malware introduced into multiple packages with 30M downloads/month each

- **Package hijacked to add backdoor targeting a specific organization** – Obfuscated malware added to a dependency which targeted a single company, went undetected for over a week, and made it into their production build

- **NPM package manager allowed anyone to publish new versions of any package** – Attackers could publish new versions of any NPM package without authorization _for multiple years_

Using third-party dependencies without proper vetting leaves you open to hacking, breaches, and assorted security misfortune.
